<header class="hero wrap">
<span class="eyebrow">UX Researcher &amp; Designer · Portfolio</span>
<h1>Designing for the people <em>waiting</em> at the bus shelter.</h1>
<p class="lead" style="margin-top:22px">A user-centred case study on the Oppidan student bus at Rhodes University: field observation, interviews, sensemaking, storyboarding, wireframes, and paper-prototype usability testing.</p>
<div class="tags"><span class="tag">Need finding</span><span class="tag">Interviews</span><span class="tag">Empathy map</span><span class="tag">Persona</span><span class="tag">Wireframing</span><span class="tag">Paper prototyping</span><span class="tag">Usability testing</span></div>
<div class="stats">
<div class="stat"><b>6</b><span>user interviews</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>8</b><span>“How might we” questions</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>5</b><span>concept sketches</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>5</b><span>usability testers</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>3</b><span>design fixes from testing</span></div>
</div>
</header>

<main class="wrap">
<section id="overview">
<span class="eyebrow">Case study · 2025</span>
<h2><i>00</i>Brief background on the Oppidan bus system</h2>
<p>The Oppidan bus system was created to understand what Oppidan students face on a regular basis, and to address gaps in the current Oppidan system as a transport service provider. It integrates the user into the decision-making process, keeping users’ needs and expectations in mind.</p>
<p>The gaps existed because students felt the experience did not cater for their needs: safety, no confusion, no frustration, schedules, and the bus drivers. The system is user-centred because it tries to understand challenges such as unpredictable schedules and the emotional discomfort of long waits.</p>
<h3>The goal and the problem</h3>
<p>The aim is a system that integrates the bus service with the student’s daily academic life. Currently, Oppidan students’ schedules and deadlines are affected, creating frustration and wasted study time. The solution is a reliable transport service built around student safety, clarity, notification and efficiency, so the bus supports the academic routine rather than disrupting it.</p>
<div class="meta">
<div><small>Project</small>Oppidan bus system redesign</div>
<div><small>Methods</small>Observation, interviews, sensemaking, storyboarding, paper-prototype testing</div>
<div><small>Output</small>Booking and tracking flow integrated into ROSS</div>
</div>
</section>

<section id="research">
<span class="eyebrow">Exercise 1</span>
<h2><i>01</i>Need finding</h2>
<h3>What, How and Why from observation</h3>
<div class="grid">
<div class="card"><span class="n">WHAT are they doing?</span><p>Using the Oppidan bus.</p><ul><li>Getting on the bus; patrolling to check seating arrangements</li><li>Arguing or fighting in the line; shouting and making noise</li><li>Benches full, people standing, line unclear</li><li>Glued to cell phones; one student on a laptop near the charging port doing an assignment</li><li>Fast-paced, rushing to the bus; rushing to the bathroom</li><li>Cuddling to keep warm; sleeping because of the weather</li><li>Some students left behind for Town and Joza to wait for the second load</li><li>The Mbuzeli town bus waiting for a set time before going to the shelter</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">HOW are they doing it?</span><p>They wait for the bus, then board when it arrives. Emotions visible in the queue:</p><ul><li>Smiles and excitement</li><li>Disappointment and frustration</li><li>Confusion and indifference</li><li>Anger and impatience</li><li>Despair and anxiety</li><li>Expectation</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">WHY are they doing it?</span><p>The bus takes them where they stay. There is no other means.</p><ul><li>The bus was full; students avoided being left behind</li><li>Securing a seat to go home on time</li><li>Patrols prevented cutting to the front</li><li>Meeting submission deadlines</li><li>Keeping warm in the cold</li><li>Long lines and an overcrowded shelter forced standing</li><li>The unclear line made students afraid to miss the bus</li><li>Passing time by distraction; drivers following a schedule</li><li>Relieving themselves before departure</li><li>Waiting beyond scheduled times</li></ul></div>
</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:50px">Interviews</h3>
<p class="lead">Six students from the Joza, Tantyi and Town routes. Tap a name to read each interview.</p>

<details class="iv"><summary>Interviewee 1</summary>
<p><b>Last time on the bus, and how it felt:</b> Yesterday (Wednesday 16 July). It was fine and on time, which was surprising because the first bus of the night is usually late. The first week of semester is usually very late. The system is time consuming with long queues. Another day the bus was 2 hours late; it was cold and she could not cook or study.</p>
<p><b>First time on the bus:</b> 2023, quite anxious. She got home on time and found it efficient, but realised it worked because she lives in town, not far from campus.</p>
<p><b>Drivers:</b> Previous drivers were rude and always late. New drivers this semester are on time, perhaps because the gap between the first and next pick-up increased. She always tells the driver her destination first and has never been brought back.</p>
<p><b>Suggestion:</b> More buses were added, meaning fewer queues, yet drivers are early and queues are still too long. Go back to the old schedule and still increase the number of buses.</p></details>

<details class="iv"><summary>Interviewee 2 · Joza</summary>
<p><b>Last time and feeling:</b> Last semester. Very stressful. Some people are bullies, including drivers, who misunderstand others’ anxiety about calling stop drops. 8 PM buses sometimes arrive at 9:30 PM, disrupting her schedule.</p>
<p><b>Why off-campus:</b> Moved to Joza and relies heavily on the bus because of financial constraints, using taxis in the morning and the bus later.</p>
<p><b>Drivers:</b> Three types: very rude, very kind and understanding, and unfamiliar with routes, leading to dangerous situations (almost falling) and expecting passengers to direct them in the dark. Some play music too loudly, so students cannot communicate their stops.</p>
<p><b>Finance and backup plans:</b> With more money she would not use the bus because the long waits waste research time. Based on what other students say, the bus would be empty if everyone could afford cabs.</p>
<p><b>Oppidan Hall committee:</b> They calm students down and call the drivers, who arrive minutes later, but drivers shout at students for calling the hall. They also guide orderly seating.</p>
<p><b>Suggestion:</b> Larger buses (like the town routes) for townships such as Joza, as a 15-seater is insufficient. The town bus comes for the second load while students still wait for the first, then Joza drivers say the delay was due to distance.</p>
<p><b>Overall:</b> Unhappy with the entire system. Students were asked to sign petitions for morning buses, which she sees as unrealistic given evening failures. Dissatisfaction is a key reason she moved back to campus.</p></details>

<details class="iv"><summary>Interviewee 3 · Town</summary>
<p><b>Last time:</b> Thursday 17 July. The bus was late and students waited long hours with no explanation from the Oppidan committee, a huge problem they face.</p>
<p><b>Impact:</b> Long waits with schoolwork to do. She arrives home very late, hurting productivity.</p>
<p><b>Committee silence:</b> She feels angry because the bus is paid for, not free. Students get no help or response and feel disrespected.</p>
<p><b>Backup plans:</b> She must pay for a cab with her very last money, an unplanned expense.</p>
<p><b>Drivers:</b> One driver is rude and impatient. He missed her stop, then got angry when reminded, claiming she had not said it earlier.</p>
<p><b>Suggestion:</b> The Oppidan committee should speak to the drivers or the person in charge of the buses so drivers are more patient with students.</p></details>

<details class="iv"><summary>Interviewee 4 · Tantyi (now Joza)</summary>
<p><b>Housing:</b> Joza now; Tantyi in the first semester. Last used the bus on the last day of last semester.</p>
<p><b>The system:</b> Not organised. With Joza’s long line, times are 5pm, 6:30pm, 8:00pm, 9:30pm and 23:00. Arriving at 5pm on the dot may still mean leaving at 8pm. To leave at 5pm, arrive at 3pm; to leave at 6pm, arrive before 5pm; arriving at 7pm for the 8pm bus means leaving at 9pm. Two buses for Joza, one for Tantyi and one for Town would make sense.</p>
<p><b>Academic impact:</b> Arriving hours early means 2 hours waiting, time that could be studying, then cooking at home. About 3 hours must be carved out of the schedule, and the bus may still be full.</p>
<p><b>Did the system fail?</b> Yes. Times clash with her schedule.</p>
<p><b>Suggestion:</b> Organisers should keep checking on students, and add buses or change times when many are waiting. When the 5pm bus takes the first 15 and leaves 15 behind, later arrivals can wait 3 to 4 hours.</p>
<p><b>Drivers:</b> No bad experience with Joza drivers. One Tantyi driver hit someone on the road, did not get out to check, fixed his mirror, joked and drove off, then drove recklessly. A first-year missed her stop and was dropped far away. Missing a stop can mean being dropped anywhere or taken back to campus and sent to the back of the line.</p></details>

<details class="iv"><summary>Interviewee 5 · Town</summary>
<p><b>About:</b> 4th-year Pharmacy student, currently Oppidan. Last used the bus Wednesday 16 July; the experience was good for her personally, though the driver is sometimes difficult.</p>
<p><b>Students:</b> Well behaved; they do not cut the line and are respectful in the queue.</p>
<p><b>Drivers:</b> Dislike stop names called out all at once. One driver does not want passengers wearing headphones. Student cards must always be shown. Drivers address issues disrespectfully (“you are a Rhodes student, you should know”). Calling stops helps the driver avoid passing them.</p>
<p><b>Timing:</b> Sometimes early, sometimes late, and sometimes they leave before the stated time (for example 20:00). Being late is a setback after an hour already going around town, and drivers treat it as normal.</p>
<p><b>Suggestion:</b> Unsure. Complaints about driver attitude have continued for a long time with no action.</p>
<p><b>Has the system failed?</b> Not really, apart from driver attitude, but it is hard for Oppidan students.</p></details>

<details class="iv"><summary>Interviewee 6 · Joza</summary>
<p><b>First experience:</b> Very long line, first come first served, so arrival at least 2 hours before the prescribed time.</p>
<p><b>Lateness and study:</b> She gets home tired.</p>
<p><b>Suggestion:</b> Designated buses for specific nearby locations.</p>
<p><b>Organisation:</b> Not organised. The bus takes only 15 passengers at a time; trips are long and the bus is small, so there are many trips. Anyone can ride; wait in the queue for a turn.</p></details>
</section>

<section id="synthesis">
<span class="eyebrow">Exercise 1 &amp; 2</span>
<h2><i>02</i>Empathy map, needs and sensemaking</h2>
<div class="two">
<figure class="fig" style="margin:0"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Empathy map with Said, Did, Thought and Felt quadrants"><figcaption>Empathy map: Said, Did, Thought, Felt</figcaption></figure>
<div><h3>Assessment of needs and insights</h3><p>Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs was used to categorise the user’s needs.</p>
<div class="bars"><div><span>Safety</span><i style="width:92%"></i></div><div><span>Esteem</span><i style="width:80%"></i></div><div><span>Self-actualisation</span><i style="width:65%"></i></div><div><span>Physiological</span><i style="width:48%"></i></div><div><span>Belonging</span><i style="width:20%"></i></div></div>
<p class="team">Bars show relative emphasis in the synthesis, not measured data.</p></div>
</div>
<div class="grid" style="margin-top:26px">
<div class="card"><span class="n">1 · PHYSIOLOGICAL</span><ul><li>Address hunger, food and cooking needs around transport, pointing to a need for time efficiency</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">2 · SAFETY</span><ul><li>Arrive safely; feel secure on commutes (for example, fear of being mugged)</li><li>All passengers accommodated</li><li>Avoid missing stops and drop-offs</li><li>Minimise cab costs caused by transport issues</li><li>Adapt to new drivers and unexpected events</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">3 · LOVE &amp; BELONGING</span><ul><li>Connecting with friends and family, or sharing experiences, is less prominent in this empathy map</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">4 · ESTEEM</span><ul><li>Receive the service they paid for and deserve</li><li>Efficient transport, with a feeling of control over time</li><li>Avoid disruptions to productivity</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">5 · SELF-ACTUALISATION</span><ul><li>Manage schedules and meet deadlines; arrive earlier than scheduled</li><li>Reduce anger, disappointment, frustration, anxiety and stress</li><li>Consider relocating for better transport</li><li>Use transit time: talking, sitting, sleeping, music, videos, reading, walking, running to the bus</li></ul></div>
</div>
<p style="margin-top:22px"><b>Primary focus.</b> Based on the “Sad”, “Felt”, “Did” and “Think” sections, users focus mainly on <b>safety needs</b> (arriving safely, feeling secure, predictability) and <b>esteem needs</b> (the service they paid for, reliability and respect), with physiological needs affected indirectly because late arrivals impair productivity. Late arrivals, disorganisation and stress directly impede users’ ability to feel safe, in control and respected.</p>

<span class="eyebrow" style="margin-top:56px">Exercise 2</span>
<h2><i>03</i>Persona, POV and ideas</h2>
<figure class="fig"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Persona: David Hlongwane, first-year Oppidan student"><figcaption>Persona: David Hlongwane, “Just trying to get by.”</figcaption></figure>
<h3 style="margin-top:34px">Point of view</h3>
<p>David Hlongwane is a first-year Oppidan student whose academic schedule is affected by long waits at the bus shelter. Every delayed ride is lost time for other activities and a growing weight of stress.</p>
<p>Oppidan students like David who rely on the bus are challenged by unpredictable wait times and unclear routes, leading to wasted study hours and emotional distress.</p>
<div class="quote">Oppidan students need reliable bus information and efficient transport to protect their valuable study time and reduce stress.</div>
<h3>How Might We questions</h3>
<ol class="hmw"><li>HMW make bus routes and stops so clear that no student ever gets confused?</li><li>HMW alleviate the emotional distress caused by long and uncertain bus waits?</li><li>HMW transform waiting for the bus into the most relaxing and joyfully anticipated part of a student’s daily journey?</li><li>HMW design a bus system that eliminates idle wait times at the shelter?</li><li>HMW make the journey and wait feel calm and time-efficient, instead of hurried and frustrating?</li><li>HMW use existing campus digital infrastructure or student networks to improve bus coordination?</li><li>HMW make the Oppi bus dependable and integrated into a student’s routine, like their academic timetable?</li><li>HMW fundamentally change the bus system to fully prioritise student academic schedules?</li></ol>
<h3 style="margin-top:30px">Brainstorming</h3>
<div class="grid">
<div class="card"><span class="n">CLEAR ROUTES AND STOPS</span><ul><li>Label buses clearly (Joza, Tantyi, Town) or give each a colour</li><li>An app to book and indicate stops, with notifications when the bus arrives early</li><li>Unique location identifiers (number plates) so users can track bookings and get notifications</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">USE CAMPUS INFRASTRUCTURE</span><ul><li>Integrate the Oppidan system into ROSS, accessible to every student anytime</li><li>A WhatsApp group for broadcast messages</li><li>Noticeboards and monitors for students without smartphones or with flat batteries</li></ul></div>
<div class="card"><span class="n">FIT THE ACADEMIC ROUTINE</span><ul><li>Emergency or late pick-ups once or twice a week for hectic submissions</li><li>Real-time bus tracking</li><li>Change pick-up or exam bus hours before swot week, not the first week of exams</li></ul></div>
</div>
<div class="card" style="margin-top:18px;border-color:var(--acc)"><span class="n">BEST SOLUTION</span><p style="margin:0">Integrate a system into ROSS where Oppidan students can book a bus ride. Students can track their bus and plan around it, so no time is wasted at the shelter, and they are constantly updated about delays.</p></div>
</section>

<section id="design">
<span class="eyebrow">Exercise 2 &amp; 3</span>
<h2><i>04</i>Concept sketches, storyboard and wireframes</h2>
<h3>Concept sketches</h3>

<section id="testing">
<span class="eyebrow">Exercise 4</span>
<h2><i>05</i>Paper prototype and usability testing</h2>
<h3>Testing script</h3>
<ol class="hmw"><li>Issue the consent form and describe its purpose.</li><li>Introduce the facilitator and team roles: facilitator, “computer” and observers.</li><li>Introduce the project: a paper prototype of an Oppidan bus system, accessed through ROSS login, to book and track a bus.</li><li>Explain the tasks: log in through ROSS, book a bus ride, track or check the booking.</li><li>Encourage thinking aloud, which shows how the user views the system in real time.</li><li>Pause between tasks so observers can ask questions.</li></ol>
<h3 style="margin-top:34px">Observations</h3>
<div class="tbl"><table><tr><th>User</th><th>Positive</th><th>Negative</th></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>Easy: login, menu, bookings page, booking a slot, view my bookings. Fast and seemed familiar with the system.</td><td>Did not notice the dashboard message or use the logout button. Unsure what to do after tracking the bus.</td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>Easy: login, menu, booking. Saw the update message. Familiar with the app.</td><td>Did not view booking information, calling it useless. Did not understand whether the tick and x removed the message or responded to it; preferred yes/no.</td></tr>
<tr><td>3</td><td>Noticed the * (required) marker. App was familiar and not confusing.</td><td>Did not understand the tracking stages; wanted simpler wording than “Outbound”. Wanted two colours on the track page for the current stage and passed stages. Clicked submit 3 times because the “computer” was slow. Skipped View my booking and wanted details like the bus number on the tracking page. No need for logout.</td></tr>
<tr><td>4</td><td>Noticed the update message.</td><td>Wanted “Outbound” changed to an understandable word. Wanted all booking information on one screen, with no view booking page. Very confused on the track page and had to think first.</td></tr>
<tr><td>5</td><td>Familiar and fast with the app.</td><td>Wanted “Outbound” and “Oppi drop-offs” simplified (for example, student drop-offs). Did not notice the update message because of its placement. Confused on the tracking page. Skipped view my booking, planning to open it only if the booked time passed without the bus arriving.</td></tr></table></div>

<h3 style="margin-top:34px">Usability problems and revised areas</h3>
<p>Three changes came out of testing: a notification page with booking details (link removed), a clearer tick-and-x replacement, and plain terminology with colour codes on the tracking page.</p>
<div class="case"><div><span class="lab b">Notification page after booking</span><p style="margin-top:12px"><b>Problem.</b> Users ignored the View my booking link, and the bus number was hidden on that page. They went straight to Track my bus and missed key details.</p><p><b>Fix.</b> Removed the view my booking link, included all relevant booking details, and kept the Track my bus link under the details.</p><p><b>Why.</b> Users have everything before tracking, with fewer clicks and quick access to booking details.</p></div>
<div class="ba"><figure><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Before"><span class="lab b">Before</span></figure><figure><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="After"><span class="lab a">After</span></figure></div></div>
<div class="case"><div><span class="lab b">Tracking stages</span><p style="margin-top:12px"><b>Problem.</b> Labels such as Outbound and Oppi drop-offs were unclear, and no colour showed whether a bus had passed or was at a stage.</p><p><b>Fix.</b> Renamed stages in friendlier words (for example, student drop-offs) and used colour to separate completed and current stages.</p><p><b>Why.</b> Confusion is removed, and progress is visible instantly.</p></div>
<div class="ba"><figure><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Before"><span class="lab b">Before</span></figure><figure><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="After"><span class="lab a">After</span></figure></div></div>
<div class="case"><div><span class="lab b">Update message</span><p style="margin-top:12px"><b>Problem.</b> The black message was missed, and users read the x as a way to close it.</p><p><b>Fix.</b> Changed the message to red and replaced tick and x with YES and NO.</p><p><b>Why.</b> Red draws attention, the words are clearer, and green for accept with red for decline guides correct engagement.</p></div>
<div class="ba"><figure><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Before"><span class="lab b">Before</span></figure><figure><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="After"><span class="lab a">After</span></figure></div></div>
</section>

<section id="reflection">
<span class="eyebrow">Reflection on the process</span>
<h2><i>06</i>What the project taught</h2>
<p>The design process was deeply insightful. It showed how a conceptual idea can evolve into a tangible, responsive solution through iterative problem-solving and user engagement. From identifying root issues to developing a dynamic paper-based prototype, analytical and creative skills grew. Observing testers interact with the prototype was particularly illuminating; each user brought a unique perspective, revealing diverse needs and prompting thoughtful refinements. The iterative feedback loop underscored the importance of inclusive design and adaptability in creating solutions that genuinely serve their intended communities.</p>
<p>Ultimately, the Oppidan bus system reflects a principled commitment to human-centred innovation, where technology and service design are functional, empathetic and empowering. The project’s success depended on determining underlying problems, understanding user demands and feelings, and creating a responsive prototype from those understandings. Flexibility and inclusive design are crucial to developing solutions that benefit the community they are designed for.</p>
</section>
